title: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complexity arises because observers are computationally equivalent to systems

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Systems with simple rules appear complex because, once a low threshold is passed, their evolution is as computationally sophisticated as any process of perception or analysis used to study them, and this holds for any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: observers will tend to be computationally equivalent to the systems they observe—with the inevitable consequence that they will consider the behavior of such systems complex.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Computational Irreducibility” (from p. 737), p. 737. Scope: observers (human or otherwise) studying systems in nature and simple programs

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.23

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Restricted observer-system pairs can be studied with existing simulations and proofs. The proposed universal causal explanation is too broad and underspecified to discriminate cleanly from alternatives such as resource bounds or poor representations.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For specified systems and observer algorithms, establish computational equivalence formally and measure prediction, compression, and classification performance. Compare with weaker observers to test whether matched computational power predicts perceived complexity in those cases.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Perceived complexity is observer- and task-dependent.

Computational equivalence does not by itself imply equal practical prediction difficulty.

The quantifier over every usable perception and analysis method is open-ended.

fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.15
operationalizability: 0.3
data adequacy: 0.1
data existence: 0.35
discriminating power: 0.2

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: There is a real proxy: standard methods predict periodic and nested cellular automata and do not compress rule 30, and both the methods and the automata are available. That proxy does not separate computational equivalence from ordinary limits of sample size, features, or effort. The general explanation, covering every usable observer and every system past a low threshold, is not fixed by those experiments.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare a computationally reducible system with an irreducible one, such as a nested cellular automaton and rule 30, using each practical analysis method as an observer. The explanation is supported if every usable method shortcuts the reducible system and fails to shortcut the irreducible one because the method is itself only Turing-powerful; it is refuted if some usable method systematically shortcuts the irreducible system.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Failure to predict can come from limited time or the wrong statistic without the observer matching the system's computational level.

Any method of perception and analysis that can actually be used already assumes the principle's bound on observers.
